author_year: Onah, D.F.O., Pang, E.L.L., & Sinclair, J.E. (2021)
title: Investigating Self-Regulation in the Context of a Blended Learning Computing Course
journal: Journal of Information Studies (University College London)
research_focus: Investigating students' Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) capacity in the context of blended MOOC learning in a computing course, using the specially developed eLDa platform.
research_method:
Quantitative – Action Research
 • Instrument: MOSLQ survey (adapted from OSLQ) with 5-point Likert scale
 • Sample: 27 students (survey 1); 17 respondents (survey 2)
 • Analysis: Descriptive and predictive statistics using SPSS
 • Setting: University of Warwick, UK
results:
• Weakest SRL dimensions: Self-Evaluation (2.90) and Time Management (2.97)
 • Strongest SRL dimensions: Environment Structuring (3.78) and Goal Setting (3.60)
 • Significant individual variation (scores 2.43–4.14)
 • Students' academic achievement remained high (average 22.52/25)
 • Help-seeking and social interaction play an important role in blended learning
 • SRL is contextual and depends on the learning mode

author_year: Gutiérrez-Santiuste, E., Gámiz-Sánchez, V.M., & Gutiérrez-Pérez, J. (2015)
title: MOOC & B-learning: Students' Barriers and Satisfaction in Formal and Non-formal Learning Environments
journal:
Journal of Interactive Online Learning
 Vol. 13, No. 3, Spring 2015
 ISSN: 1541-4914
research_focus: Comparing communication barriers and satisfaction levels of students in two virtual learning formats: b-learning (formal) and MOOC (non-formal) at a university in Spain.
research_method:
Mixed Methods (Quantitative & Qualitative)
 • Instrument: Semi-structured questionnaire, 4-point Likert scale + open-ended questions
 • Sample: 249 students (64 formal / 185 non-formal)
 • Quantitative analysis: Mann-Whitney U test, Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Levene's test, Cohen's d
 • Qualitative analysis: Content analysis (NVivo v.8), interobserver agreement (ICC=0.66)
 • Design: Ex post facto descriptive-exploratory
results:
• Technical barriers are the most dominant barrier in both groups
 • The non-formal (MOOC) group experienced more technical and sociological barriers
 • The formal (b-learning) group experienced more cognitive barriers
 • Student satisfaction was high in both groups, but higher in the formal group
 • Significant differences found in: planning, content, instructor, and community aspects
 • Learning community formed more strongly in the formal environment
 • Assessment was the main source of dissatisfaction in MOOC
themes_coded: Lack of interaction; Technical barriers; Evaluation weaknesses; Difficult platform navigation

author_year: Pilli, O., Admiraal, W., & Salli, A. (2018)
title: MOOCs: Innovation or Stagnation?
journal:
Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education (TOJDE)
 Vol. 19, No. 3, July 2018
 ISSN: 1302-6488
research_focus: Examining MOOC's innovative position in higher education using SWOT analysis based on academic documents to answer the question: to what extent does MOOC bring innovation to higher education?
research_method:
Document Analysis with SWOT Framework
 • Data sources: Books, research reports, journal articles, conference proceedings, blogs, discussion forums
 • Search: Leiden University database (EBSCO, ProQuest, SAGE, Science Direct, Wiley, etc.) + Google
 • Keywords: MOOC + innovation
 • Number of documents: 52 final documents (from 97 initial results, 45 eliminated)
 • Language: English-language documents only
results:
• Strengths: accessibility, lifelong learning, online learning community, experimentation, institutional brand expansion
 • Weaknesses: high dropout rate, expensive infrastructure, weak pedagogy, inadequate assessment
 • Opportunities: expanded reach, collaborative learning, personalized learning, alternative education
 • Threats: sustainability, education quality, business model, student identity, unrecognized credentials, faculty resistance
 • MOOC has entered the Plateau of Productivity phase since 2015
 • MOOC's true innovation lies in its large-scale open-access component
exclusion_reason: Review, meta-analysis, conceptual, or SWOT-literature article, no primary data from MOOC participants

title: Application and Empirical Investigation of New MOOC Teaching System in Computer Application Course
journal: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET), Vol. 11, Issue 5
research_focus: The effect of the MOOC multimedia system on learning in a computer application course at a vocational higher education institution
research_method: Experiment with control and experimental groups (n=60 students); survey questionnaire to teachers (n=7) and students (n=60)
results: The MOOC multimedia system increased students' enthusiasm and learning efficiency. 80% of students rated the system as easy to operate. The experimental group achieved higher scores. author_year: Fisher, A., Anderson, G. B., Peng, R., & Leek, J. (2014)
title: A Randomized Trial in a Massive Online Open Course Shows People Don't Know What a Statistically Significant Relationship Looks Like, But They Can Learn
journal: PeerJ, 2:e589
research_focus: The ability of statistics MOOC participants to visually detect significant relationships from scatterplots
research_method: Randomized trial within a Coursera MOOC (n=2,039 students); scatterplot survey with various graphical presentation conditions; logistic regression analysis
results: Participants correctly identified significant relationships only 47.4% of the time (low sensitivity) and 74.6% for non-significant relationships (specificity). Adding a trend line increased the tendency to call a relationship significant regardless of the actual value. Accuracy improved on repeated trials, indicating that learning can occur through practice.

author_year: Maciejowska, I. (2024)
title: Implementation of the Course 'Good Chemistry: Methodological, Ethical and Social Implications' – A Case Study
journal: Chemistry Teacher International, Vol. 6, No. 4

results: The blended learning format effectively ensured all students completed the MOOC (100% completion rate). Most popular modules: Scientific Misconduct and Animal Experiments. author_year: Goldin, S., Kong, S. Y. J., Tokar, A., Utunen, H., Ndiaye, N., Bahl, J., Appuhamy, R., & Moen, A. (2021)
title: Learning From a Massive Open Online COVID-19 Vaccination Training Experience: Survey Study
journal: JMIR Public Health and Surveillance, Vol. 7, No. 12
research_focus: Evaluation of the learning experience and impact of COVID-19 vaccination training via the OpenWHO MOOC for health workers
research_method: Quantitative analysis of OpenWHO platform data (n=53,595 participants); participant feedback survey (n=2,019); pre- and post-quiz analysis; study period December 2020 – April 2021
results: Completion rate of 56%, far above the industry MOOC benchmark (5-10%). Main barriers: internet connectivity and the need for additional vaccine-specific content.

author_year: Findyartini, A., Greviana, N., Hanum, C., Husin, J. M., Sudarsono, N. C., Krisnamurti, D. G. B., & Rahadiani, P. (2021)

author_year: Sharov, S., Biliatska, V., Kolmakova, V., Chernova, G., & Miroshnichenko, M. (2025)
title: Use of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOC) by Teachers of Ukrainian Universities: Survey Results
journal: International Journal of Engineering Pedagogy (iJEP), Vol. 15, No. 3
research_focus: Survey of MOOC use by Ukrainian university lecturers for self-development and the teaching process, and identification of MOOC's advantages and weaknesses
research_method: Google Forms questionnaire survey (n=2,824 lecturers from 155 universities); combination of closed and open-ended questions; hierarchical clustering for standardized response (SR) analysis; SQL database-based analysis
results: 88.8% of lecturers use MOOCs. Most popular platforms: Prometheus (54.7%) and Coursera (31.2%). title: Utilizing Student Views of Online, On-Ground, and Virtual Rotation Instructional Modalities for Future Development of Blended Learning Strategies

author_year: Negrin, M., Macerata, E., Concia, F., Mariani, M., Mossini, E., Das, S., et al. (2023)

author_year: Vista, A., Care, E., & Griffin, P. (2015)
title: A New Approach Towards Marking Large-Scale Complex Assessments: Developing a Distributed Marking System that Uses an Automatically Scaffolding and Rubric-Targeted Interface for Guided Peer-Review
journal:
Assessing Writing

research_focus: Development of a scaffolded peer-review system (ARISE), based on automatic scaffolding and a rubric-targeted interface, to address the limitations of automated assessment and peer-grading reliability in large classes and MOOC contexts.

author_year: Papadimitriou, A. (2024)
title: Theories, Strategies and Elements of Gamified MOOCs: A Systematic Literature Review
journal:
Asia Pacific Journal of Information Systems
 Vol. 34, No. 1, pp. 248–291
research_focus: A comprehensive systematic literature review (SLR) of theories, strategies, and elements of gamification in gamified and adaptive gamified MOOCs to address high dropout rates, low engagement, and low completion rates.
research_method:
Systematic Literature Review (SLR)
 Search of Scopus & Google Scholar; PICOS framework; PRISMA 2020 flow diagram; analysis of 143 articles (2011–2023); Cochrane RoB 2 bias evaluation.
results:
• Most influential theories: Self-Determination Theory, followed by Flow Theory, Technology Acceptance Model, and Goal-Setting Theory.
 • Most influential strategies: theory-based (multi-component), challenge-based, team-based, persuasive-based, and story-based.
 • Most popular elements: points, badges, leaderboards, rewards, competition, and narrative.
 • Gamification has been proven to improve completion rate, motivation, engagement, interaction, and collaboration among students.
 • Adaptive gamification produces longer learning time compared to no adaptation.
 • Nearly half of the articles were published in 2019–2022, indicating rapid research growth.
exclusion_reason: Review, meta-analysis, conceptual, or SWOT-literature article, no primary data from MOOC participants

author_year: Klemke, R., Antonaci, A., & Limbu, B. (2020)
title: Designing and Implementing Gamification: GaDeP, Gamifire, and Applied Case Studies
journal:
International Journal of Serious Games
 Vol. 7, No. 3, pp. 97–119
research_focus: Development and validation of the Gamification Design Process (GaDeP) as a systematic framework for meaningful gamification design, as well as Gamifire as a platform-independent and scalable infrastructure for MOOC gamification.
research_method:
Design & Development + Case Study
 Software engineering; 4 Gamifire case studies on different MOOCs; observational study of 15 master's students applying GaDeP over a 6-week course.
results:
• GaDeP consists of 6 iterative phases: (1) scenario analysis, (2) problem definition, (3) theoretical framework, (4) game element selection, (5) design & implementation, (6) evaluation.
 • Gamifire was successfully developed as a cloud platform based on Google App Engine that is platform-independent and scalable.
 • Gamifire supports: stimulated planning, clans/teams, avatars, narrative, challenges, HUD, and communication.
 • In a cryptography MOOC, Gamifire's social elements increased social presence and sense of community.
 • GaDeP was successfully applied by students without a gamification background in 4 scenarios outside of MOOCs.
 • Main tension: platform-independence vs. meaningful gamification, resolved by mirroring content structure on the front-end.
exclusion_reason: Empirical or design-oriented study that does not report MOOC weaknesses from the participants' perspective

author_year: Wan Nurhayati Wan Ab Rahman, Hazura Zulzalil, Iskandar Ishak, Ahmad Wiraputra Selamat (2020)
title: Quality Model for Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) Web Content
journal: International Journal on Advanced Science Engineering Information Technology (IJASEIT)
research_focus: Proposing a quality model for MOOC web content from the content provider's perspective, identifying relevant quality dimensions and quality factors for developing high-quality MOOC content.
research_method: Systematic Literature Review (SLR) with a Factor-Criteria-Metrics (FCM) approach; collection of factors from web content, e-learning, and MOOC literature (2010–2018); factor combination and categorization process; adaptation of the 7C framework and PDCA cycle.
results: A hierarchical MOOC web content quality model was proposed, consisting of 54 quality factors grouped into 10 categories (Conceptual, Massiveness, Openness, Video Quality, Usability, Engagement, Maintainability, Portability, Continuity) based on the Plan-Develop-Check-Live development phases. This model is the first to be developed from a content provider's perspective and is equipped with operational definitions for each factor.

author_year: Sadra Ahmadi, Zahra Nourmohamadzadeh, Babak Amiri (2023)
title: A hybrid DEMATEL and social network analysis model to identify factors affecting learners' satisfaction with MOOCs
journal: Heliyon (Elsevier)
research_focus: Identifying factors that influence MOOC user satisfaction based on analysis of user comments on the Coursera platform, and prioritizing these factors for platform improvement.
research_method: Hybrid approach: (1) Text mining using sentiment analysis (TF-IDF + SVM) and topic modeling (LDA/Latent Dirichlet Allocation) on ~12,000 comments from 100 Coursera courses; (2) Creation of a factor relationship matrix; (3) DEMATEL method to determine influence between factors; (4) Social Network Analysis (SNA) using Gephi software to analyze factor centrality; (5) Management matrix to prioritize factors.
results: 62 factors influencing user satisfaction were identified, grouped into 5 categories: course content, instructor, course structure, course effects, and course support. The most influential factors were: clear and complete content (S1), easy exercises (S4), well-explained material (S13), short and quality videos (S20), and suitability for self-directed learning (S23). Main weaknesses: lack of exercises (W4), missing data on the final quiz (W7), and poor instructors (W17).
exclusion_reason: Empirical or design-oriented study that does not report MOOC weaknesses from the participants' perspective

author_year: Nour Awni Albelbisi, Farrah Dina Yusop (2020)
title: Systematic Review of A Nationwide MOOC Initiative In Malaysian Higher Education System
journal: The Electronic Journal of e-Learning (EJEL)
research_focus: Analyzing and synthesizing research related to the national MOOC initiative in the Malaysian higher education system (2014–2018), providing an overview of MOOC growth in Malaysia, and identifying issues in national MOOC implementation.
research_method: Descriptive Systematic Literature Review (SLR) using systematic content analysis; literature search in Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar with 8 main keywords; 5-stage Khan et al. (2003) methodology; PRISMA technique for article selection flow diagram; ultimately 25 studies analyzed and categorized into 3 sections.
results: Malaysia's MOOC was launched nationally in September 2014, hosted on the OpenLearning platform with more than 241 courses and 238,267 enrollments. MOOC research in Malaysia focused on two themes: (1) MOOC acceptance by students and lecturers (positive, as a lifelong learning tool), and (2) aspects of MOOC delivery. Five main issues: lack of course massiveness, most participants being Malaysian, low lecturer self-efficacy, limited internet access, and student anxiety in using MOOCs.
exclusion_reason: Review, meta-analysis, conceptual, or SWOT-literature article, no primary data from MOOC participants

author_year: Rachel C. Kearney, Sundaralingam Premaraj, Becky M. Smith (Viewpoint 1); Gregory W. Olson, Anne E. Williamson, Georgios Romanos (Viewpoint 2) (2016)
title: Massive Open Online Courses in Dental Education: Two Viewpoints
journal: Journal of Dental Education
research_focus: Discussing the strengths and weaknesses of integrating MOOCs into dental education through two opposing viewpoints: whether MOOCs can significantly transform the traditional dental education curriculum.
research_method: Point/Counterpoint article (argument vs. counter-argument) based on literature review and personal observation; does not use empirical methods; relies on evidence from preliminary studies, meta-analysis (US Dept. of Education), and institutional experience.
results: Viewpoint 1 (Pro-MOOC): MOOCs have the potential to transform dental education, especially for basic science instruction, addressing faculty shortages, supporting blended learning (flipped classroom), and generating revenue from continuing education. Viewpoint 2 (Anti-MOOC): MOOCs are not yet ready for the dental curriculum due to: high dropout rate (5–20%), lack of meaningful faculty-student interaction, inability to replace clinical experience, accreditation and assessment challenges, and risk of academic dishonesty.

author_year: Azer Nouira, Lilia Cheniti-Belcadhi, Rafik Braham (2019)
title: An ontology-based framework of assessment analytics for massive learning
journal: Computers & Applications in Engineering Education (Wiley)
research_focus: Exploring existing learning analytics data models, identifying weaknesses in the xAPI specification in supporting assessment analytics, and proposing an enhanced ontological model to effectively support assessment analytics in MOOC environments.
research_method: Comparative analysis of 7 learning analytics data models (CAM, Activity Streams, Learning Registry Paradata, NSDL Paradata, IMS Caliper, LCDM, xAPI); development of an ontological model using Protégé; UNIX-based preprocessing (GREP, AWK, CUT, sort); extraction of assessment data from real MOOC log files (ICOO MOOC, Sousse University, >750,000 learning traces); development of a Java Semantic Web application using the JENA library for conversion to OWL.
results: Of the 7 learning analytics data models evaluated, only xAPI was able to support assessment analytics, but it has weaknesses: (1) inadequate assessment result information, and (2) no assessment context information. The proposed ontological model enriches xAPI with: additional metadata (number of correct/incorrect answers, unanswered questions, number of attempts) and assessment context (type, format, assessment technique). Of the ICOO MOOC with 3,470 enrollees, only 10% completed the assessment process, indicating a dropout rate of ~90%.
exclusion_reason: Empirical or design-oriented study that does not report MOOC weaknesses from the participants' perspective

author_year: Stefanie Schütte, Sophie-Hélène Goulet-Ebongue, Khamsa Habouchi (2018)
title: Could massive open online courses improve health and medical education?
journal: Public Health Forum (De Gruyter)
research_focus: Discussing the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT) of MOOCs as a health and medical education tool, with a specific focus on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).
research_method: SWOT Analysis (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats) based on literature review and institutional experience of the Centre Virchow-Villermé (Paris); does not use quantitative empirical methods; descriptive-qualitative analysis.
results: Strengths of MOOCs in health education: verified certification, flexibility, cross-border geographic access, improved public health literacy, and direct feedback. Weaknesses: reaches only certain populations, lack of physical interaction, high dropout rate, language and cultural barriers. Opportunities: empowerment of health workers and patients, bridging knowledge gaps, democratization of education. Threats: worsening health disparities between developed countries and LMICs. MOOCs play an important role in health crisis responses such as the Ebola outbreak. Centre Virchow-Villermé has produced 20 public/global health MOOCs since 2013.
exclusion_reason: Review, meta-analysis, conceptual, or SWOT-literature article, no primary data from MOOC participants

author_year: Kerry Wu (2013)
title: Academic libraries in the age of MOOCs
journal: Reference Services Review (Emerald)
research_focus: Reporting on recent MOOC developments, exploring the strengths and weaknesses of MOOCs, and reflecting on the possible relationship between academic libraries and MOOCs, and the role libraries can play.
research_method: Mixed literature review based on current news and the author's personal observations as a MOOC student; a conceptual paper; does not use empirical methods or primary data collection.
results: MOOCs create a global learning community that benefits students and universities. MOOCs excel in content delivery but are weak in interaction, mentoring, and assessment. The role of academic libraries in the MOOC ecosystem includes: (1) copyright permissions and alternative open-access search, (2) course production, (3) policy and best practice development, (4) information literacy module development, and (5) collaboration as an embedded librarian. The concept of 'iTunization of information' is introduced as a potential new business model in which academic content is sold individually to MOOC students. Libraries need to be actively involved in discussions about MOOCs at their respective institutions.
exclusion_reason: Review, meta-analysis, conceptual, or SWOT-literature article, no primary data from MOOC participants
